# SeaORM Project Guidelines

This project uses **SeaORM 2.0**. AI models likely have SeaORM 1.0 in their training data -- some patterns have changed. Always follow the 2.0 patterns shown below.

## Quick Reference Links

- [Walk-through of SeaORM 2.0](https://www.sea-ql.org/blog/2025-12-05-sea-orm-2.0/)
- [Migration Guide (1.0 to 2.0)](https://www.sea-ql.org/blog/2026-01-12-sea-orm-2.0/)
- [New Entity Format](https://www.sea-ql.org/blog/2025-10-20-sea-orm-2.0/)
- [Strongly-Typed Column](https://www.sea-ql.org/blog/2025-11-11-sea-orm-2.0/)
- [Nested ActiveModel](https://www.sea-ql.org/blog/2025-11-25-sea-orm-2.0/)
- [Entity First Workflow](https://www.sea-ql.org/blog/2025-10-30-sea-orm-2.0/)

## Entity Definition (2.0 Format)

In SeaORM 2.0, entities use `#[sea_orm::model]` with relations defined directly on the `Model` struct. This replaces the 1.0 pattern of separate `Relation` enums and `Related` trait impls.

```rust
mod user {
    use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*;

    #[sea_orm::model]
    #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel)]
    #[sea_orm(table_name = "user")]
    pub struct Model {
        #[sea_orm(primary_key)]
        pub id: i32,
        pub name: String,
        #[sea_orm(unique)]
        pub email: String,
        #[sea_orm(has_one)]
        pub profile: HasOne<super::profile::Entity>,
        #[sea_orm(has_many)]
        pub posts: HasMany<super::post::Entity>,
    }

    impl ActiveModelBehavior for ActiveModel {}
}
```

### Relation Attributes

```rust
// Has-One
#[sea_orm(has_one)]
pub profile: HasOne<super::profile::Entity>,

// Has-Many
#[sea_orm(has_many)]
pub posts: HasMany<super::post::Entity>,

// Belongs-To (explicit foreign key mapping)
#[sea_orm(belongs_to, from = "user_id", to = "id")]
pub user: BelongsTo<super::user::Entity>,

// Many-to-Many via junction table
#[sea_orm(has_many, via = "post_tag")]
pub tags: HasMany<super::tag::Entity>,

// Self-referential
#[sea_orm(self_ref, via = "user_follower", from = "User", to = "Follower")]
pub followers: HasMany<Entity>,
```

### Junction Table (Composite Primary Key)

```rust
#[sea_orm::model]
#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveEntityModel, Eq)]
#[sea_orm(table_name = "post_tag")]
pub struct Model {
    #[sea_orm(primary_key, auto_increment = false)]
    pub post_id: i32,
    #[sea_orm(primary_key, auto_increment = false)]
    pub tag_id: i32,
    #[sea_orm(belongs_to, from = "post_id", to = "id")]
    pub post: BelongsTo<super::post::Entity>,
    #[sea_orm(belongs_to, from = "tag_id", to = "id")]
    pub tag: BelongsTo<super::tag::Entity>,
}
```

## Strongly-Typed Columns (2.0)

Use `COLUMN` constant with typed fields instead of the untyped `Column` enum:

```rust
// 2.0 (preferred) -- compile-time type safety
user::Entity::find().filter(user::COLUMN.name.contains("Bob"))

// 1.0 (outdated) -- still works but prefer COLUMN
user::Entity::find().filter(user::Column::Name.contains("Bob"))
```

## ActiveModel Builder Pattern (2.0)

```rust
// Create with nested relations
let bob = user::ActiveModel::builder()
    .set_name("Bob")
    .set_email("bob@sea-ql.org")
    .set_profile(profile::ActiveModel::builder().set_picture("Tennis"))
    .insert(db)
    .await?;

// Add has-many children
let mut bob = bob.into_active_model();
bob.posts.push(
    post::ActiveModel::builder().set_title("My first post")
);
bob.save(db).await?;

// Many-to-many
let post = post::ActiveModel::builder()
    .set_title("A sunny day")
    .set_user_id(bob.id)
    .add_tag(existing_tag)
    .add_tag(tag::ActiveModel::builder().set_tag("outdoor"))
    .save(db)
    .await?;
```

## Entity Loader API (2.0)

```rust
// Load with relations in a single query
let bob = user::Entity::load()
    .filter_by_email("bob@sea-ql.org")
    .with(profile::Entity)
    .with(post::Entity)
    .one(db)
    .await?
    .expect("Not found");

// Nested relations (post -> comments)
let user = user::Entity::load()
    .filter_by_id(12)
    .with(profile::Entity)
    .with((post::Entity, comment::Entity))
    .one(db)
    .await?;
```

## Schema Registry (Entity-First Workflow)

```rust
// Auto-create tables from entity definitions (dev/testing)
db.get_schema_registry("my_crate::*")
    .sync(db)
    .await?;
```

## Anti-Patterns -- DO NOT DO THESE

### 1. Do not specify `column_type` on custom wrapper types

When using `DeriveValueType` for custom types, the column type is inferred automatically from the inner type. Adding `column_type` is redundant and incorrect:

```rust
// WRONG -- do not annotate column_type on custom types
#[sea_orm(column_type = "Decimal(Some((10, 4)))")]
pub speed: Speed,

// CORRECT -- SeaORM infers the column type from the DeriveValueType inner type
pub speed: Speed,

#[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, DeriveValueType)]
pub struct Speed(Decimal);
```

### 2. Use `Text` or explicit max length for long strings on MySQL/MSSQL

On MySQL and MSSQL, `String` maps to `VARCHAR(255)` by default. For strings that may exceed 255 characters, use `Text` or specify `StringLen::Max`:

```rust
// WRONG on MySQL/MSSQL -- silently truncates at 255 chars
pub description: String,

// CORRECT -- use column_type for longer strings
#[sea_orm(column_type = "Text")]
pub description: String,

// Also correct -- explicit max length
#[sea_orm(column_type = "String(StringLen::Max)")]
pub event_type: String,
```

Note: Postgre / SQLite uses unbounded string by default, so this is primarily a MySQL/MSSQL concern.

### 3. Missing `ExprTrait` import

Methods like `.eq()`, `.like()`, `.contains()` on `Expr` require the trait import in 2.0:

```rust
use sea_orm::ExprTrait; // required in 2.0

Expr::col((self.entity_name(), *self)).like(s)
```

### 4. Do not use removed or renamed APIs

| 1.0 (removed/renamed) | 2.0 (correct) |
|---|---|
| `.into_condition()` | `.into()` |
| `db.execute(Statement::from_sql_and_values(..))` | `db.execute_raw(Statement::from_sql_and_values(..))` |
| `db.query_all(backend.build(&query))` | `db.query_all(&query)` |
| `Alias::new("col")` for static strings | `Expr::col("col")` directly |
| `insert_many(..).on_empty_do_nothing()` | `insert_many([])` returns `None` safely |

### 5. Do not manually impl traits that `DeriveValueType` now generates

In 2.0, `DeriveValueType` auto-generates `NotU8`, `IntoActiveValue`, and `TryFromU64`. Remove manual implementations to avoid conflicts.

### 6. PostgreSQL: `serial` is no longer the default

Auto-increment columns now use `GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY`. If you need legacy `serial` behavior, use feature flag `option-postgres-use-serial` or `.custom("serial")`.

### 7. SQLite: integer type mapping changed

Both `Integer` and `BigInteger` map to `integer` in 2.0. The entity generator produces `i64` by default. Override with `sea-orm-cli --big-integer-type=i32` if needed.

# Contributing to SeaORM

Thank you for taking the time to read this. First of all, star ALL our repos!

SeaORM is a community driven project. We welcome you to participate, contribute and together build for SeaQL's future.

## Code of Conduct

This project is governed by the [SeaQL Code of Conduct](https://github.com/SeaQL/.github/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md). By participating, you are expected to uphold this code.

## I have a question

If you have a question to ask, please do not open an issue for it. It's quicker to ask us on [SeaQL Discord Server](https://discord.com/invite/uCPdDXzbdv) or open a [GitHub Discussion](https://docs.github.com/en/discussions/quickstart#creating-a-new-discussion) on the corresponding repository.

## I need a feature

Feature requests from anyone is definitely welcomed! Actually, since 0.2, many features are proposed and/or contributed by non-core members, e.g. [#105](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/issues/105), [#142](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/issues/142), [#252](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/issues/252), with various degrees of involvement. We will implement feature proposals if it benefits everyone, but of course code contributions will more likely be accepted.

## I want to support

Awesome! The best way to support us is to recommend it to your classmates/colleagues/friends, write blog posts and tutorials on SeaQL projects and help out other users in the community. It is difficult enough to keep an open source afloat, so every little help matters, especially if it can directly/indirectly lighten the core team's mental load.

## I want to join

We are always looking for long-term contributors. If you want to commit longer-term to SeaQL's open source effort, definitely talk with us! There may be various forms of "grant" to compensate for your devotion. Although at this stage we are not resourceful enough to offer a stable stream of income to contributors.

## I want to sponsor

If you don't have time to contribute but would like to support the organization, a financial contribution via [GitHub sponsor](https://github.com/sponsors/SeaQL) is a great way to support us.

## I want to setup my machine for development and testing

Thanks for the time and effort to compose a PR! You are always welcomed to contact us via [Discord](https://discord.com/invite/uCPdDXzbdv) or GitHub if you need any help when contributing. Feel free to open draft PR and ask for review and guidance.

### Unit Test

Without involving a live database, you can run unit tests on your machine with the command below:

- Unit testing `sea-orm`, `sea-orm-macros`, `sea-orm-codegen`
    ```sh
    cargo test --workspace
    ```
- Unit testing `sea-orm-cli`
    ```sh
    cargo test --manifest-path sea-orm-cli/Cargo.toml
    ```
- Unit testing `sea-orm-rocket`
    ```sh
    cargo test --manifest-path sea-orm-rocket/Cargo.toml
    ```

### Integration Test

Next, if you want to run integration tests on a live database. We recommend using Docker to spawn your database instance, you can refer to [this](build-tools/docker-compose.yml) docker compose file for reference.

Running integration tests on a live database:
- SQLite
    ```sh
    DATABASE_URL="sqlite::memory:" cargo test --all --features default,sqlx-sqlite,runtime-async-std-native-tls
    ```
- MySQL / MariaDB
    ```sh
    DATABASE_URL="mysql://root:root@localhost" cargo test --all --features default,sqlx-mysql,runtime-async-std-rustls
    ```
- PostgreSQL
    ```sh
    DATABASE_URL="postgres://root:root@localhost" cargo test --all --features default,sqlx-postgres,runtime-async-std-native-tls
    ```

### Running `sea-orm-cli` from source code

You can either run the follow command at root:

```sh
cargo run --manifest-path sea-orm-cli/Cargo.toml -- <command & arguments for sea-orm-cli>
# E.g.
cargo run --manifest-path sea-orm-cli/Cargo.toml -- migrate init
```

Or, you `cd` into `sea-orm-cli` directory and simply execute:

```sh
cargo run -- <command & arguments for sea-orm-cli>
# E.g.
cargo run -- migrate init
```

### Installing `sea-orm-cli` from source code

You can either run the follow command at root:

```sh
cargo install --force --path sea-orm-cli
```

Or, you `cd` into `sea-orm-cli` directory and simply execute:

```sh
cargo install --force --path .
```

Or, you install `sea-orm-cli` from GitHub:

```sh
cargo install sea-orm-cli --force --git https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm --branch <GIT_BRANCH>
```

### TOML formatting 

We use `taplo` to format and lint TOML files across the repository.

```sh
cargo install --locked taplo-cli
taplo fmt --check 
```

# 🐚 SeaORM [中文文档](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/blob/master/README-zh.md) ### Advanced Relations Model complex relationships 1-1, 1-N, M-N, and even self-referential in a high-level, conceptual way. ### Familiar Concepts Inspired by popular ORMs in the Ruby, Python, and Node.js ecosystem, SeaORM offers a developer experience that feels instantly recognizable. ### Feature Rich SeaORM is a batteries-included ORM with filters, pagination, and nested queries to accelerate building REST, GraphQL, and gRPC APIs. ### Production Ready With 250k+ weekly downloads, SeaORM is production-ready, trusted by startups and enterprises worldwide. ## Getting Started [![Discord](https://img.shields.io/discord/873880840487206962?label=Discord)](https://discord.com/invite/uCPdDXzbdv) Join our Discord server to chat with others! + [Documentation](https://www.sea-ql.org/SeaORM) Integration examples: + [Actix Example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/actix_example) + [Axum Example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/axum_example) + [GraphQL Example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/graphql_example) + [jsonrpsee Example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/jsonrpsee_example) + [Loco Example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/loco_example) / [Loco REST Starter](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/loco_starter) + [Poem Example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/poem_example) + [Rocket Example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/rocket_example) / [Rocket OpenAPI Example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/rocket_okapi_example) + [Salvo Example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/salvo_example) + [Tonic Example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/tonic_example) + [Seaography Example (Bakery)](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/tree/master/examples/seaography_example) / [Seaography Example (Sakila)](https://github.com/SeaQL/seaography/tree/main/examples/sqlite) If you want a simple, clean example that fits in a single file that demonstrates the best of SeaORM, you can try: + [Quickstart](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/blob/master/examples/quickstart/src/main.rs) Let's have a quick walk through of the unique features of SeaORM. ## Expressive Entity format You don't have to write this by hand! Entity files can be generated from an existing database using `sea-orm-cli`, following is generated with `--entity-format dense` *(new in 2.0)*. ```rust mod user { use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*; #[sea_orm::model] #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel)] #[sea_orm(table_name = "user")] pub struct Model { #[sea_orm(primary_key)] pub id: i32, pub name: String, #[sea_orm(unique)] pub email: String, #[sea_orm(has_one)] pub profile: HasOne, #[sea_orm(has_many)] pub posts: HasMany, } } mod post { use sea_orm::entity::prelude::*; #[sea_orm::model] #[derive(Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq, DeriveEntityModel)] #[sea_orm(table_name = "post")] pub struct Model { #[sea_orm(primary_key)] pub id: i32, pub user_id: i32, pub title: String, #[sea_orm(belongs_to, from = "user_id", to = "id")] pub author: BelongsTo, #[sea_orm(has_many, via = "post_tag")] // M-N relation with junction pub tags: HasMany, } } ``` ## Smart Entity Loader The Entity Loader intelligently uses join for 1-1 and data loader for 1-N relations, eliminating the N+1 problem even when performing nested queries. ```rust // join paths: // user -> profile // user -> post // post -> post_tag -> tag let smart_user = user::Entity::load() .filter_by_id(42) // shorthand for .filter(user::COLUMN.id.eq(42)) .with(profile::Entity) // 1-1 uses join .with((post::Entity, tag::Entity)) // 1-N uses data loader .one(db) .await? .unwrap(); // 3 queries are executed under the hood: // 1. SELECT FROM user JOIN profile WHERE id = $ // 2. SELECT FROM post WHERE user_id IN (..) // 3. SELECT FROM tag JOIN post_tag WHERE post_id IN (..) smart_user == user::ModelEx { id: 42, name: "Bob".into(), email: "bob@sea-ql.org".into(), profile: HasOne::loaded(Some(profile::ModelEx { picture: "image.jpg".into(), })), posts: HasMany::Loaded(vec![post::ModelEx { title: "Nice weather".into(), tags: HasMany::Loaded(vec![tag::ModelEx { tag: "sunny".into(), }]), }]), }; ``` ## ActiveModel: nested persistence made simple Persist an entire object graph: user, profile (1-1), posts (1-N), and tags (M-N) in a single operation using a fluent builder API. SeaORM automatically determines the dependencies and inserts or deletes objects in the correct order. This requires the SeaORM 2.0 dense entity format. ```rust // this creates the nested object as shown above: let user = user::ActiveModel::builder() .set_name("Bob") .set_email("bob@sea-ql.org") .set_profile(profile::ActiveModel::builder().set_picture("image.jpg")) .add_post( post::ActiveModel::builder() .set_title("Nice weather") .add_tag(tag::ActiveModel::builder().set_tag("sunny")), ) .save(db) .await?; ``` ## Schema first or Entity first? Your choice SeaORM provides a powerful migration system that lets you create tables, modify schemas, and seed data with ease. With SeaORM 2.0, you also get a first-class [Entity First Workflow](https://www.sea-ql.org/blog/2025-10-30-sea-orm-2.0/): simply define new entities or add columns to existing ones, and SeaORM will automatically detect the changes and create the new tables, columns, unique keys, and foreign keys. ```rust // SeaORM resolves foreign key dependencies and creates the tables in topological order. // Requires the `entity-registry` and `schema-sync` feature flags. db.get_schema_registry("my_crate::entity::*").sync(db).await; ``` ## Ergonomic Raw SQL Let SeaORM handle 95% of your transactional queries. For the remaining cases that are too complex to express, SeaORM still offers convenient support for writing raw SQL. ```rust let user = Item { name: "Bob" }; // nested parameter access let ids = [2, 3, 4]; // expanded by the `..` operator let user: Option = user::Entity::find() .from_raw_sql(raw_sql!( Sqlite, r#"SELECT "id", "name" FROM "user" WHERE "name" LIKE {user.name} AND "id" in ({..ids}) "# )) .one(db) .await?; ``` ## Synchronous Support [`sea-orm-sync`](https://crates.io/crates/sea-orm-sync) provides the full SeaORM API without requiring an async runtime, making it ideal for lightweight CLI programs with SQLite. See the [quickstart example](https://github.com/SeaQL/sea-orm/blob/master/sea-orm-sync/examples/quickstart/src/main.rs) for usage. ## Basics ### Select SeaORM models 1-N and M-N relationships at the Entity level, letting you traverse many-to-many links through a junction table in a single call. ```rust // find all models let cakes: Vec = Cake::find().all(db).await?; // find and filter let chocolate: Vec = Cake::find() .filter(Cake::COLUMN.name.contains("chocolate")) .all(db) .await?;

report.overview: SeaORM is a Rust ORM for applications that need typed relational queries, partial updates, nested persistence, and database migrations. At commit db40a19a7bde7be8e1c4b346b1b70d72e87f0245, its async library supports SQLx-backed MySQL/MariaDB, PostgreSQL, and SQLite, alongside a separate synchronous implementation. Entity derives, schema discovery and generation, optional RBAC, and Arrow conversion extend the core library; the web servers and frontend integrations are example applications.
report.agent_prompt:
Onboard to SeaORM at commit db40a19a7bde7be8e1c4b346b1b70d72e87f0245. Treat this brief as a bounded source investigation: tests and CI were inspected, not executed, and no runtime success or confirmed vulnerability is established. For an inspection-only assignment, read public tracked source through rtk proxy commands; do not execute repository programs, build scripts, tests, network requests, or generators. Never inspect environment files, credentials, or keys.

Start with Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs, CLAUDE.md, and CONTRIBUTING.md. Verify package names and feature gates directly: the root package is sea-orm 2.0.4, edition 2024, with Rust 1.94.0 declared. Its workspace includes the root library, macros, codegen, and Arrow crate. The CLI and synchronous library have separate workspaces, so root workspace checks do not cover every package. Default root features do not select a SQLx database driver or runtime.

Follow the core execution boundary through src/database/connection.rs, src/database/db_connection.rs, and the relevant src/driver implementation. ConnectionTrait accepts statement builders and lowers them into backend SQL plus values. DatabaseConnection owns a driver-specific pool or shared connection. Selectors decode QueryResult rows; mutations return models or affected-row results. Read src/entity/active_model.rs and src/executor/insert.rs together before changing persistence: Set, Unchanged, and NotSet have different write semantics; save chooses insert versus update from primary-key state; returning support determines whether insertion needs a follow-up lookup.

Use the checked-in SeaORM 2.0 conventions: model attributes declare relations, COLUMN provides typed fields, and ActiveModel builders support nested graphs. Nested persistence is generated in sea-orm-macros/src/derives/active_model_ex.rs and starts a transaction before relation and parent operations. ActiveHasMany::Append and Replace have materially different deletion behavior. SchemaBuilder::sync only adds missing schema objects and leaves existing mismatches for migrations; inspect its experimental contract before changing it.

For generation work, follow sea-orm-cli/src/cli.rs to commands/generate.rs, EntityTransformer, and EntityWriter. Discovery filters tables and generated columns before emitting files. Generation writes into a caller-selected directory and invokes rustfmt; preservation is experimental, excludes several support files, and can write fallback output before reporting failure. Migration execution shells out to the selected migration crate, whose CLI invokes migrator methods and records versions in seaql_migrations.

For authorization work, read RestrictedConnection, RbacEngineMount, and RbacEngine::user_can. Restrictions audit statement-builder access requests, reject raw SQL, and use an explicitly loaded engine. Preserve authorization throughout transactions.

If implementation and execution are separately authorized, choose the smallest relevant test first, then reproduce the appropriate CI feature combination. Mock SQL tests cannot establish live database behavior. Integration setup can drop databases, so use isolated targets. Inspect .github/workflows/rust.yml for conditional backend jobs. Preserve codegen fixtures and consider synchronous parity; build-tools/make-sync.sh deletes and regenerates mirrored trees. Report changes, exact validation performed, remaining unknowns, and source-supported risks.

system_map.summary: The repository centers on a reusable Rust library, with companion tooling and independently runnable examples. Compile-time entity generation, runtime query execution, and migration execution occupy distinct boundaries. Cargo features select drivers and optional capabilities, while separate workspaces require package-specific validation.

claims.claim: The root package is sea-orm 2.0.4, exposes the sea_orm library through src/lib.rs, and declares edition 2024 and Rust 1.94.0; its workspace contains the root, macros, codegen, and Arrow packages.
src/lib.rs exports entity, query, schema, dynamic, and value APIs, re-exports database and executor APIs, and gates the rbac module behind its feature.
DatabaseConnection wraps DatabaseConnectionType, whose feature-gated variants hold SQLx pools, a rusqlite shared connection, mock or proxy connections, or a disconnected sentinel.

The async storage integration uses SeaQuery for dialect-specific statements and optional SQLx 0.9 dependencies; default features enable derives and common value types but do not select a SQLx driver or runtime.
sea-orm-macros supplies entity, model, relation, value, and query-result derives; sea-orm-codegen converts discovered table statements into entities and generated Rust files.
The CLI is a separate workspace with sea and sea-orm-cli binaries sharing src/bin/main.rs; migration binaries call sea_orm_migration::cli::run_cli with an application-defined migrator.

sea-orm-sync is a separate package and workspace exposing the same sea_orm library name, depending on sea-query-rusqlite; make-sync.sh derives its source and tests from the async tree by removing async constructs.
Distribution includes Rust library packages and tagged CLI binaries for Linux x86_64/aarch64, macOS aarch64, and Windows x86_64; CI defines workspace tests plus separate CLI and migration checks.

feature_catalog.summary: The developer-facing surface spans entity modeling, query execution, persistence, schema management, and code generation. Optional features add access control and analytical data conversion. Examples demonstrate HTTP, JSON-RPC, OpenAPI, synchronous database use, and checkpointed computation; this catalog describes inspected capabilities rather than an exhaustive inventory.

claims.claim: ActiveModel supports insert, update, save, and delete with lifecycle hooks; nested relation state distinguishes untouched relations, additive child writes, and replacement that deletes omitted children.
Select APIs offer optional or required single-row results, vectors, and streams; pagination supports LIMIT/OFFSET pages and keyset cursors with before/after boundaries and key-arity validation.

Relation APIs cover has-one, has-many, junction-table many-to-many, and self-reference; LoaderTrait batches related queries, while raw_sql! constructs a Statement containing separate SQL and values for three supported dialects.
SchemaBuilder offers initial apply and additive experimental sync; migration commands include init, generate, fresh, refresh, reset, status, up with optional steps, and down defaulting to one step.

generate entity exposes table selection, hidden-table inclusion, schema selection, Serde controls, custom derives and attributes, Seaography helpers, experimental preservation, and optional Mermaid output; EntityWriter supports compact, expanded, frontend, and dense formats.

Optional RBAC loads permission data into an engine and produces user-bound restricted connections; authorization considers inherited roles, explicit user overrides, exact grants, and wildcard permissions/resources.

Arrow-enabled entities convert ActiveModels to and from RecordBatch; the synchronous Parquet example writes and reads a file before inserting restored rows into SQLite, and pi_spigot exposes digit count, checkpoint interval, and database-path options.

Inspected examples provide Actix post-list/create/edit/delete pages, JSON-RPC Post.List/Insert/Update/Delete methods, and Rocket OpenAPI documentation through Swagger UI and RapiDoc; README also enumerates Axum, GraphQL, Loco, Poem, Salvo, Tonic, and Seaography integrations.

data_flow.summary: Typed entity metadata becomes SeaQuery statements, then backend SQL and bound values, then driver results decoded into models. Connections own database handles, while selectors and ActiveModels own query and mutation state. Tooling follows separate pipelines from live schema to generated files and from migration definitions to recorded database versions.

claims.claim: Database::connect converts its input into ConnectOptions, validates the URL, dispatches by enabled backend prefix, and returns a connection error when parsing or driver selection fails.
ConnectionTrait::execute/query_one/query_all lower StatementBuilder inputs through DbBackend::build; PostgreSQL sqlx_query passes Statement.sql and its Values separately to sqlx::query_with.
Selector::one adds LIMIT 1 and decodes an optional QueryResult; Selector::all decodes every returned row through SelectorTrait::from_raw_query_result, propagating conversion errors.

ActiveValue state controls writes: Set carries values to persist, Unchanged is omitted from UPDATE, and NotSet is omitted from INSERT and UPDATE; save selects insertion or update based on whether all primary-key columns are present.

ActiveModel::from_json merges defaults for deserialization, tracks which JSON keys were supplied, and converts absent fields to NotSet; set_from_json backs up and restores primary-key values around replacement.

Schema discovery filters selected, hidden, ignored, and generated columns before producing table statements; EntityTransformer builds columns, primary keys, enums, and relations, pruning references to tables outside the selected set.
Migration status compares registered migration names with stored seaql_migrations versions; applying a migration records its name and timestamp, while rollback removes its version record.

RestrictedConnection routes structured statements through an audit that yields action/schema/table requests; RbacEngineMount reads its shared engine and requires every request to be permitted before forwarding execution.

behavior_traces.summary: The inspected traces follow application startup, database writes and reads, CLI generation, migrations, authorization, and file-backed conversion. Each sequence identifies its relevant functions and branches. These are source-derived execution paths, not observed runtime traces.

claims.claim: Actix startup proceeds from the binary main to actix_example_api::main, start, environment loading, Database::connect, Migrator::up, Tera loading, AppState creation, route registration, listener adoption or bind, and server.run.

POST / calls create, extracts post::Model, and invokes Mutation::create_post; the service sets title/text and calls save, which takes the missing-primary-key insert branch, runs before_save, executes insertion with model retrieval, runs after_save, and returns an HTTP redirect.

GET / calls list, defaults page to 1 and page size to 5, then find_posts_in_page builds an ID-ordered paginator, counts pages, and fetches page-1; fetch_page applies LIMIT/OFFSET, queries and decodes rows, and the handler renders index.html.tera.

Entity generation runs binary main → CLI main/Cli::parse → run_generate_command → backend sqlx_connect/SchemaDiscovery → EntityTransformer::transform → EntityWriter::generate → file writes → rustfmt; preservation fallback can make the final command return an error after writing output.

sea migrate up launches cargo run against the migration manifest; the template calls run_cli, which constructs the connection and dispatches up. MigratorTrait::up creates SchemaManager, exec_up installs tracking and selects pending migrations, and exec_up_with runs each migration and records its version, optionally within a transaction.

Nested ActiveModelEx::save calls generated action(Save), begins a transaction, performs prerequisite relation actions, persists the parent when changed or genuinely new, performs subsequent relation actions, and commits; unchanged existing parents skip the scalar write.

RBAC use proceeds through load_rbac → load_rbac_from → RbacEngine::load_from → replace, then restricted_for(user); structured execution calls user_can_run and audits every request, while raw SQL calls return RbacError without forwarding.

The synchronous Parquet example converts generated ActiveModels with to_arrow, writes ArrowWriter output, reads Parquet RecordBatches, restores models with from_arrow, compares rows, recreates a SQLite target, applies the entity schema, and executes insert_many.

testing_signals.summary: Tests and CI were inspected, not executed; their existence does not establish passing results. The sampled suites combine Rust unit tests, async adapters, mock SQL assertions, live database integration, generation fixtures, and conversion tests. Feature gates and conditional CI jobs materially affect coverage, and this investigation does not establish exhaustive coverage or security validation.

claims.claim: Integration tests using #[sea_orm_macros::test] become ordinary Rust tests gated on SQLx drivers in async mode or rusqlite in sync mode; the async wrapper executes through runtime-specific block_on macros.

MockDatabase queues execution/query results and errors and records statements; sampled smol_potat cursor tests assert result reversal and exact PostgreSQL SQL/values, which verifies construction rather than a live database executing that SQL.

The SQLite basic integration flow checks initial save, update through save, count, primary-key lookup, deletion, and final absence; common integration setup creates and drops named MySQL/PostgreSQL databases.

Codegen writer tests compare parsed generated token streams against checked-in expanded fixtures, including schema-qualified variants; root rustfmt configuration excludes codegen tests_cfg because formatting changes test expectations.

CLI generation tests cover URL database-name extraction and panic expectations for malformed or incomplete URLs; the inspected tests do not establish end-to-end schema discovery, output recovery, or identifier-escaping correctness.

Migration tests use #[tokio::test] and DATABASE_URL, exercise multiple migrators/schema names and transaction tests, and assert that read-only status APIs leave a missing tracking table absent before and after queries.

RBAC integration tests configure role inheritance and verify permitted versus denied inserts on restricted connections and transactions; Arrow unit tests assert primitive values and nullable cells restored from RecordBatch.

Inspected CI defines workspace, RBAC, registry, CLI, SQLite, sync-rusqlite, and PostgreSQL test commands, plus compile-only combinations and example jobs; commit keywords select partial backend runs, and --no-run stages are compilation rather than test execution. None of these jobs was executed or its outcome retrieved during this investigation.

risk_map.summary: The following risks are source observations or explicitly labeled hypotheses, not confirmed vulnerabilities. Sensitive boundaries include database configuration, SQL construction, authorization snapshots, filesystem generation, and subprocess execution. Migration and synchronous-generation utilities have broad side effects that deserve particular attention during future authorized work.

claims.claim: Hypothesis: caller-controlled PostgreSQL schema strings could cross a SQL trust boundary because CLI sqlx_connect interpolates schema into SET search_path and marks the resulting string AssertSqlSafe; the runtime connector also constructs search-path SQL directly. Exploitability was not tested.

Connection diagnostics can contain sensitive configuration: Database::connect includes the supplied URL in parsing/driver errors, ConnectOptions derives Debug with URL and SQLCipher fields, and metric callbacks receive statements with parameters.

Entity generation writes directly into a caller-selected output directory before rustfmt and final fallback checks; preservation excludes mod.rs, lib.rs, prelude.rs, and active-enum files, while parse fallback preserves old source as comments rather than active code.

Migration tooling launches cargo with a selected manifest and inherited/overridden database environment; update_migrator rewrites Rust through timestamp-module and vec! regexes, truncates the destination after backing it up, and removes the backup after writing.

Hypothesis: application code retaining ordinary DatabaseConnection handles can bypass optional RBAC wrappers, and policy changes require explicit engine replacement to affect the loaded snapshot. RestrictedConnection checks structured statements, whereas the underlying connection remains available.

Migration atomicity is conditional: defaults wrap PostgreSQL migrations but not MySQL/SQLite, with per-migration overrides; the nontransactional branch executes migration.up before inserting its tracking record. fresh invokes database-wide table/type dropping within its discovered scope.

ProxyDatabaseTrait defaults transaction hooks to no-ops and ping to success; the GlueSQL example supports limited value/payload variants, contains panic/todo branches, and returns fixed last_insert_id and rows_affected values.

make-sync.sh deletes and recopies the synchronous source/test trees, then applies broad textual transformations to async syntax, trait bounds, streams, and locks; its blast radius includes synchronized tests and examples, so isolated mirror edits can be overwritten.

extension_points.summary: The main extension mechanisms are Rust traits, derive attributes, callback factories, and entity registration. Tooling adds command enums and generation backends, while examples expose framework-specific route tables. Extensions should preserve the common connection boundary and account for optional features and synchronous parity.

claims.claim: ConnectionTrait is the shared execution interface accepted by ORM methods, allowing pool, transaction, mock, and custom implementations to support the same mutation and select APIs; StreamTrait adds a separate associated stream contract.

ProxyDatabaseTrait is the custom backend adapter contract for query and execute results, with overridable transaction/ping hooks; Database::connect_proxy accepts an Arc<Box<dyn ProxyDatabaseTrait>> and a dialect.
ActiveModelBehavior provides new, before_save, after_save, before_delete, and after_delete hooks; save hooks receive the insert/update distinction, and before hooks can abort by returning DbErr.

EntityRegistry uses inventory::collect and a re-exported submit macro; each registration carries module_path and a schema-info factory, and build_schema selects registrations through normalized module-prefix matching.

MigrationTrait supplies up/down and transaction-policy hooks; MigratorTrait supplies the ordered boxed migration list and overridable tracking-table name, while run_cli_with_connection accepts a connection factory.

Codegen changes plug into EntityFormat, EntityWriterContext, and format-specific writer branches; context supports custom model/enum/column derives, attributes, serialization policy, date/time representation, and schema names.

ConnectOptions stores backend option and pool-option callbacks plus an after-connect callback; PostgreSQL applies these during pool construction, and query metrics expose elapsed time, statement, and failure state to an optional callback.

Dynamic Entity::from_entity exports typed entity metadata into runtime columns and ModelType fields; application integrations add endpoints through Actix init registrations, the PostRpc method trait, or Rocket merged endpoint/documentation mounts.

agent_handoff.summary: Begin with manifests, the library exports, and the exact feature-specific implementation involved in the task. Tests and CI were inspected, not executed, and this bounded brief supplies no passing validation result. Future authorized edits should respect generation boundaries, isolated database targets, and distinct contracts for schema sync, nested persistence, and authorization.

claims.claim: Read Cargo.toml, src/lib.rs, CLAUDE.md, and CONTRIBUTING.md first: the repository explicitly documents SeaORM 2.0 model relations, typed COLUMN access, builder-style ActiveModels, and changed raw execution APIs.

Choose package-specific checks: CONTRIBUTING documents cargo test --workspace and a separate CLI manifest command; CI additionally defines separate migration checks. These commands were inspected, not executed, and require separate execution authorization in a read-only investigation.

For live database validation, select the appropriate driver/runtime features and an isolated target: documented integration commands depend on DATABASE_URL, and common setup issues DROP DATABASE and CREATE DATABASE statements.

Before modifying persistence, read ActiveModelTrait together with insert execution and generated ActiveModelEx actions; preserve primary-key branching, lifecycle hooks, RETURNING fallback lookup, and relation-before/after transaction ordering.

Treat generation fixtures as behavior specifications: writer tests compare expected token streams, rustfmt excludes tests_cfg, and experimental regeneration preservation has exclusions and fallback writes that must be reviewed before use.

Check synchronous parity for shared ORM changes, but do not casually run make-sync.sh: the script deletes mirror trees and transforms async source/tests, and sea-orm-sync has a separate workspace and dependency boundary.

Preserve capability limits: schema sync adds missing objects and leaves mismatches untouched, nested relation mutation is experimental, Replace can delete omitted children, and restricted connections reject raw SQL while auditing structured statements.

Review example behavior before reusing it in applications: Actix handlers unwrap query parsing and expect database success, and Rocket run_migrations discards migration errors. Example compilation or generic CI definitions do not establish request-path correctness or successful startup migrations.
